title: Human Rights
summary: Learn the foundations of human rights: what they are and where they come from, the UN treaty system, the African human rights system including the Banjul Charter and Maputo Protocol, key rights in practice, protecting groups at risk, and remedies and advocacy.
audience: Students, activists, community workers, journalists, officials and anyone who wants to understand and defend rights

body.p: Human rights are the basic rights and freedoms that belong to every person simply because they are human, regardless of nationality, sex, ethnicity, religion, language, disability or any other status. They are universal, inalienable (they cannot be taken away, though some may be limited by law), indivisible and interdependent: the right to health, for example, depends on rights to water, food and information.

Ideas of dignity and justice exist in many traditions, including African ideas of community and ubuntu, often summarised as "a person is a person through other persons". After the horrors of the Second World War, the United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) in 1948, which became the foundation of modern international human rights law.

list: Civil and political rights: life, liberty, freedom from torture, fair trial, expression, assembly and participation in government.
Economic, social and cultural rights: work, education, health, housing, food, water and social security.
Collective or peoples' rights: development, peace and a satisfactory environment, emphasised in African human rights law.

body.tip: Rights come with duties: states must respect, protect and fulfil rights, and individuals must respect the rights of others.

body.p: The UDHR is a declaration, but many of its principles are now binding through treaties that states choose to ratify.

list: The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR), both adopted in 1966.
The Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW).
The Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC).
The Convention against Torture and the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.

body.p: Each treaty has a committee of experts that reviews reports from states and, where states accept it, individual complaints. The UN Human Rights Council conducts the Universal Periodic Review, in which every UN member's record is examined by other states. Special rapporteurs investigate themes and countries. Civil society organisations submit shadow reports to give an independent view.

body.tip: Find out which treaties your country has ratified; ratification creates obligations your government can be held to.

body.p: Africa has its own regional system under the African Union.

list: The African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Banjul Charter) was adopted in 1981 and came into force in 1986. It protects individual rights and peoples' rights, and also sets out duties of individuals towards family, community and the state.
The African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights, based in Banjul, The Gambia, promotes rights, examines state reports and hears complaints (communications).

The African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights, based in Arusha, Tanzania, issues binding judgments. Individuals and NGOs can only bring cases directly if their state has made a special declaration accepting this.
The Maputo Protocol (2003) protects the rights of women, including rights relating to violence, marriage, property and reproductive health.
The African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child has its own expert committee.

body.p: Sub-regional courts, such as the ECOWAS Court of Justice and the East African Court of Justice, have also decided human rights cases.

body.tip: African Commission decisions and Court judgments are published online and are useful for advocacy and study.

body.p: Discrimination means treating people unfairly because of characteristics such as race, sex, ethnicity, religion or disability. Equality may also require positive measures, such as accessible buildings or programmes for historically excluded groups.

list: No one may be arbitrarily detained; people arrested must be told why, be able to see a lawyer and be brought before a court quickly.
Torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment are prohibited in all circumstances.
Everyone is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

body.p: Freedom of expression and media freedom let people criticise government and expose wrongdoing. Limits, such as on incitement to violence or hate speech, must be clear, necessary and proportionate. Internet shutdowns have been widely criticised by human rights bodies as disproportionate restrictions.

body.tip: When a right is limited, ask whether the limit is set by law, pursues a legitimate aim and is proportionate.

list: Women and girls: protection from gender-based violence, child marriage and harmful practices; equal rights to land, inheritance and political participation.
Children: rights to education, protection from abuse and child labour, birth registration, and to be heard in matters affecting them.
Persons with disabilities: accessibility, inclusive education and the right to make their own decisions.
Refugees and internally displaced persons: the right not to be returned to danger (non-refoulement); the AU's Kampala Convention protects internally displaced people.
Older persons, minorities, indigenous peoples and people living with HIV, who often face stigma and discrimination.

body.p: Intersectionality recognises that people can face several forms of discrimination at once, such as a girl with a disability in a rural area.

Companies also have responsibilities. The UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights say states must protect, businesses must respect and victims must have access to remedies, relevant to mining, agriculture and supply chains.

body.tip: Always centre the voices of affected people when documenting or advocating on rights issues.

body.p: Rights matter only if violations can be remedied.

steps: Document the violation: what happened, when, where, who was involved, witnesses, photos, medical reports, kept securely and with consent.
Use local remedies: complain to the police, the relevant ministry, a national human rights commission or ombudsman, or go to court.
Seek legal help from legal aid bodies, university law clinics or human rights organisations.
If local remedies fail or are unavailable, consider regional or international bodies.
Use advocacy: media, community mobilisation, petitions and engaging officials.

body.p: National human rights institutions exist in most African countries and can investigate complaints, often for free.
Human rights defenders can face threats. Protect sources and personal data, assess risks before publishing, and know where to get help.

body.tip: Regional and international bodies usually require you to try local remedies first; keep records showing you did.
